harmonic-oscillator-elevator~perturbatio.story:
A real spring is never perfectly harmonic: stretch it far enough and the force law changes. We model that by adding a small extra term to the oscillator Hamiltonian, here $\lambda x^4$. Perturbation theory says: if the extra term is small, the energy of level $|n\rangle$ shifts by the average of the extra term in that state, $E_n^{(1)}=\lambda\langle n|x^4|n\rangle$.

The remaining problem is computing $\langle n|x^4|n\rangle$. That is where room A (the elevator) comes in. Write the position as $x=\sqrt{\hbar/2m\omega}\,(a+a^\dagger)$. Then $x^4$ is a sum of products of four ladder operators. Each $a^\dagger$ moves the state up one rung, each $a$ down one rung. To get back to the same $|n\rangle$ you need two ups and two downs, in every possible order, and each path has a weight $\sqrt{n}$ or $\sqrt{n+1}$ from the ladder rules. Counting the paths gives $3(\hbar/2m\omega)^2(2n^2+2n+1)$.

So ladder operators are a bookkeeping device that turns an integral into counting steps. The same operator $x^4$ also connects $n$ to $n\pm2$ and $n\pm4$, which matters at second order.
harmonic-oscillator-elevator~perturbatio.example: For the ground state ($n=0$), $2n^2+2n+1=1$ and the shift is $3\lambda\hbar^2/(4m^2\omega^2)$. For $n=10$ the factor is $221$, so the shift is $221$ times larger. The correction grows like $n^2$ because highly excited states swing out to large $|x|$, where $x^4$ is big, so the perturbation stops being small.
harmonic-oscillator-elevator~perturbatio.remember: First-order shift = average of the perturbation in the level; ladder operators evaluate $\langle n|x^4|n\rangle$ by counting up and down steps, giving $2n^2+2n+1$.

angular-momentum-spin~hydrogen-lamp.story:
An electron orbiting a nucleus is a tiny current loop, so it is a magnet. Its magnetic moment points opposite to its orbital angular momentum: $\boldsymbol\mu=-\mu_B\mathbf L/\hbar$. In a field $B$ along $z$ the energy of this magnet is $E_Z=\mu_BB\,m_l$, where $m_l=-l,\dots,+l$ is the $z$-component of $L$ in units of $\hbar$. So a level with angular momentum $l$ splits into $2l+1$ equally spaced sublevels (room A).

In room B the hydrogen atom emits a line when the electron jumps between levels. With the field on, both the starting and final levels split, so the line splits. For H$\alpha$ the allowed jumps have $\Delta m_l=0,\pm1$, which gives three lines in the "normal Zeeman effect": one unshifted ($\pi$) and two shifted by $\pm\mu_BB$ ($\sigma_\pm$). The shift in wavelength follows from $\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2\Delta E/(hc)$.

When the electron spin is included, the real splitting pattern has more lines (the "anomalous" Zeeman effect) because the spin has $g\approx2$, not $1$. The simple three-line picture holds when spin is ignored or cancels, as in singlet states.
angular-momentum-spin~hydrogen-lamp.example: At $B=1$ T, $\mu_BB=58\ \mu$eV. For H$\alpha$ ($656.3$ nm) $\Delta\lambda=\lambda^2\mu_BB/(hc)=0.020$ nm, a very small shift compared with $656$ nm. In a strong sunspot field of $0.3$ T the shift is only $0.006$ nm, yet it is measurable with a good spectrograph; the Earth's field of $50\ \mu$T gives a million times less than the lab $1$ T.
angular-momentum-spin~hydrogen-lamp.remember: In a field each orbital level splits into $2l+1$ sublevels with $E=\mu_BB\,m_l$, so a spectral line splits into $\pi$ and $\sigma_\pm$ components.

spin-addition-stern-gerlach~entanglement.story:
Two spin-1/2 particles can be combined into total spin $S=0$ or $S=1$. The $S=0$ state is the singlet, $\frac1{\sqrt2}(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)$. Room A derives it with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients as the one combination that has zero total spin.

Room B reads the same state as an experiment. Notice that this state cannot be written as one state for particle 1 times one state for particle 2: it is entangled. Neither particle has a definite spin by itself, but the pair has: total spin zero means that, whatever axis you measure, the two results are opposite. If Alice finds up along an axis, Bob finds down along the same axis, every time. This perfect anticorrelation alone could be mimicked by classical dice that are pre-set at the source.

The surprise comes when the two measure along different axes. The singlet predicts the correlation $E(\hat a,\hat b)=-\hat a\cdot\hat b=-\cos\theta$. No pre-set classical answers can reproduce this for all angles: the CHSH combination of correlations reaches $2\sqrt2$ in quantum mechanics but never exceeds $2$ in any local classical model.
spin-addition-stern-gerlach~entanglement.example: Alice measures along $z$, Bob along an axis tilted by $60^\circ$. The correlation is $E=-\cos60^\circ=-0.5$. With results $\pm1$, $E=P(\text{same})-P(\text{opposite})$, so $P(\text{opposite})=(1+0.5)/2=75\%$ and $P(\text{same})=25\%$. At $\theta=0$ you get $100\%$ opposite, at $90^\circ$ a $50/50$ chance.
spin-addition-stern-gerlach~entanglement.remember: The singlet ($S=0$) cannot be factorised, so it is entangled: opposite results on every common axis and correlations $-\cos\theta$ (CHSH $=2\sqrt2>2$).

hydrogen-lamp~perturbation-forge.story:
The simple Schroedinger solution gives hydrogen energies $E_n$ that depend only on $n$: many different states share one energy (they are degenerate). Real atoms have small corrections of relative size $\alpha^2\approx5\times10^{-5}$ (relativistic motion and spin-orbit coupling), where $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant. These are the perturbation $H'$.

Room B explains the method for a degenerate level: ordinary perturbation theory has a problem (denominators of $E_n-E_n=0$), so you must first find the right combinations of states within the degenerate subspace, those in which $H'$ is diagonal. The trick: pick the basis where $H'$ is already diagonal. For the spin-orbit term $\propto\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf S$ this is the coupled basis $|n,l,j,m_j\rangle$, because $\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf S$ commutes with $J^2$ but not with $L_z$ or $S_z$. Room A then just reads off the result: the shift depends on $n$ and $j$, $E^{(1)}_{nj}=E_n\frac{\alpha^2}{n^2}\Big(\frac{n}{j+1/2}-\frac34\Big)$.

So the $n=2$ level splits into $2p_{3/2}$ above and $2p_{1/2}$ below, the "fine structure" (and $2s_{1/2}$ stays with $2p_{1/2}$ at this order).
hydrogen-lamp~perturbation-forge.example: The $2p_{3/2}$-$2p_{1/2}$ splitting is $\frac{\alpha^2}{4}|E_2|=4.5\times10^{-5}$ eV, i.e. $10.9$ GHz. Relative to the H$\alpha$ photon energy of $1.89$ eV that is $2.4\times10^{-5}$, so the red line at $656.3$ nm is split by about $0.016$ nm, comparable to the Zeeman shift in a $1$ T field.
hydrogen-lamp~perturbation-forge.remember: Degenerate perturbation theory: use the basis where $H'$ is diagonal. For spin-orbit that is $|n,l,j,m_j\rangle$, and the energy depends on $j$.

fermi-sea~degenerate-matter.story:
In a degenerate Fermi gas almost every electron is stuck: all states below the Fermi energy $E_F$ are full, so an electron cannot absorb a little heat energy because there is nowhere to go. Only electrons within about $k_BT$ of $E_F$ have empty states just above them. That is a fraction of order $T/T_F$ of all the electrons. So the electron heat capacity is only $C_{el}=\frac{\pi^2}{2}Nk_B\,T/T_F$, much smaller than the classical $\tfrac32Nk_B$.

Room A is a metal: the Sommerfeld result. For copper $T_F=8.2\times10^4$ K, so at $300$ K the fraction is tiny and $C_{el}$ is only about $2\%$ of $Nk_B$. Room B is the interior of a white dwarf: the same electron gas with a much larger $T_F\sim10^9$ K. It acts as a stiff, nearly heat-less source of pressure. The heat sits in the ions, which are a classical gas with $C=\tfrac32Nk_B$.

The consequence: the star cools through its ions. The degenerate electrons hold the star up without storing much heat. Same: only a thin shell of electrons takes part in heat. Different: how far below $T_F$ you are.
fermi-sea~degenerate-matter.example: In copper at $300$ K: $C_{el}/Nk_B=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\cdot\frac{300}{8.2\times10^4}=0.018$. In a white dwarf at $10^7$ K with $T_F\approx10^9$ K, the ratio is $\frac{\pi^2}{2}\cdot10^{-2}\approx0.05$. In both cases electrons contribute only a few percent of the classical value, and the ions dominate the heat capacity in the star.
fermi-sea~degenerate-matter.remember: Only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $E_F$ can take up heat, a fraction $T/T_F$: so $C_{el}\propto T$ is small, in metals and white dwarfs alike.

bonding-grotto~tunneling-bridge.story:
Imagine two identical valleys separated by a hill. A particle placed in the left valley is not really stuck: its wave leaks through the hill, so over time it slowly sloshes to the right valley and back. The true energy states are not "left" and "right" but the symmetric (even) and antisymmetric (odd) combinations. The even one has no node at the hill and has the lower energy; the odd one has a node and is higher. The gap between them is $\Delta E=2t$ and it is set by how well the wave tunnels through the hill: $t\propto e^{-\kappa d}$ for barrier width $d$.

Room A (bonding grotto) is the same picture for two atoms. The valleys are the two atomic orbitals $|a\rangle$, $|b\rangle$ and $t$ is the transfer integral. The even combination $|+\rangle=(|a\rangle+|b\rangle)/\sqrt2$ is the bonding orbital, lower by $t$, and the odd combination is the antibonding orbital, higher by $t$. If two electrons occupy the bonding orbital, the molecule gains energy and the atoms are bound.

The bond length is a balance: bringing atoms closer increases $t$, but at very short distances the repulsion of the nuclei wins.
bonding-grotto~tunneling-bridge.example: The particle in a double well oscillates between the wells with period $h/\Delta E=h/(2t)$. If $2t=0.1$ eV, the period is $4.1\times10^{-14}$ s, about $41$ fs. If the barrier gets wider by $1$ angstrom, with $\kappa=1$ per angstrom, $t$ drops by $e^{-1}=0.37$ and the oscillation slows to about $110$ fs.
bonding-grotto~tunneling-bridge.remember: A bond is a split double well: the even (bonding) state lies lower by $t$, the odd one higher by $t$, and $t$ is the tunnelling amplitude $\propto e^{-\kappa d}$.

bonding-grotto~hydrogen-lamp.story:
To build a molecule you can start from what you know: the hydrogen atom. LCAO means "linear combination of atomic orbitals". Take the 1s orbital $\phi_a$ on atom A and $\phi_b$ on atom B and guess that the molecule's electron is in $\psi=c_a\phi_a+c_b\phi_b$. For two identical atoms the two solutions are the sum and the difference of $\phi_a$ and $\phi_b$.

The orbitals are not orthogonal: they overlap, $S=\langle\phi_a|\phi_b\rangle$. For two hydrogen 1s orbitals at distance $R$ one can calculate it exactly: $S=e^{-R/a_0}(1+R/a_0+R^2/3a_0^2)$. It is $1$ at $R=0$ and falls to $0$ for large $R$. The resulting energies are $E_\pm=(H_{aa}\pm H_{ab})/(1\pm S)$. Here $H_{aa}$ is the energy of the electron on one atom (including the attraction to the other nucleus), and $H_{ab}$, the exchange integral, is negative.

Because of the denominator $1\pm S$ the antibonding level is pushed up more than the bonding level is pushed down. That is why two helium atoms (filling both levels) do not bind.
bonding-grotto~hydrogen-lamp.example: At $R=2.5\,a_0$ (about $1.3$ angstrom) the overlap is $S=e^{-2.5}(1+2.5+2.083)=0.46$, so the denominators are $1.46$ for the bonding state and $0.54$ for the antibonding state. The same numerator is divided by a smaller number for the antibonding level, so it ends up above the unperturbed level by more than the bonding one ends up below.
bonding-grotto~hydrogen-lamp.remember: LCAO: the molecule's orbitals are sums and differences of atomic 1s orbitals; the overlap $S$ makes the antibonding level rise more than the bonding one falls.

semiconductor-forge~fermi-sea.story:
The Fermi-Dirac function $f(E)=1/(e^{(E-\mu)/k_BT}+1)$ tells you the chance that a state of energy $E$ is occupied, with $\mu$ the chemical potential. For energies far above $\mu$, with $E-\mu\gg k_BT$, the $+1$ in the denominator becomes negligible and $f\approx e^{-(E-\mu)/k_BT}$: the classical Boltzmann factor. The Pauli principle matters little when states are mostly empty.

In a metal (Fermi sea) $\mu\approx E_F$ lies inside a band, so states below it are nearly full and above it nearly empty. This is the degenerate case, and the number of electrons $n\approx8.5\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ (copper) barely depends on temperature. In a semiconductor $\mu$ lies in the gap, far from the conduction band edge $E_c$. The few electrons in the conduction band are dilute and obey Boltzmann statistics: $n=N_c\,e^{-(E_c-\mu)/k_BT}$. With $\mu$ in the middle of the gap, the number of carriers is $n_i\propto T^{3/2}e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$ ($E_g$ is the gap), which depends very strongly on temperature.

Same function, two limits: degenerate (step function) in metals, non-degenerate (exponential tail) in semiconductors.
semiconductor-forge~fermi-sea.example: For intrinsic silicon, $E_g=1.12$ eV, heating from $300$ K to $400$ K multiplies $n_i$ by $e^{0.56\text{ eV}/k_B\,(1/300-1/400)\text{ K}^{-1}}\times(4/3)^{3/2}\approx e^{5.4}\times1.5\approx350$. For copper the electron density does not change at all, which is why metals get slightly worse conductors when hot (more scattering) while semiconductors get better.
semiconductor-forge~fermi-sea.remember: The Fermi-Dirac function becomes a Boltzmann exponential when $E-\mu\gg k_BT$: a semiconductor has such a tail, a metal has a sharp Fermi step.

lattice-gate~formalism-and-uncertainty.story:
A symmetry gives a conserved quantity, and in quantum mechanics a conserved quantity means a commuting operator. If the Hamiltonian is unchanged when you shift by a distance $a$, the translation operator $T_a=e^{-i\hat pa/\hbar}$ commutes with $H$: $[H,T_a]=0$. Then $H$ and $T_a$ can be diagonalised together, and the eigenstates of $H$ can be chosen to be eigenstates of $T_a$ as well, with eigenvalue $e^{-ika}$ (just a phase, since $T_a$ is unitary).

A crystal is not invariant under every shift but only under shifts by lattice vectors $\mathbf R$. This is enough: $[H,T_{\mathbf R}]=0$ for those, and the result is Bloch's theorem, $\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)$. The wave vector $\mathbf k$ is a label for the eigenvalue of translation, called the crystal momentum. It is not the true momentum, because $\hat p$ does not commute with $H$ in a periodic potential.

Since $e^{ika}=e^{i(k+2\pi/a)a}$, $k$ and $k+2\pi/a$ give the same eigenvalue, so you only need $k$ in one Brillouin zone, $-\pi/a<k\le\pi/a$.
lattice-gate~formalism-and-uncertainty.example: Take a ring of $N=4$ atoms. Translating by one lattice constant four times returns to the start, so $(e^{ika})^4=1$ and the eigenvalue of $T_a$ can only be $1,i,-1,-i$. These are four distinct values, so four allowed $k$ in the Brillouin zone: $k=0,\pm\pi/2a,\pi/a$. In general, $N$ atoms give $N$ allowed $k$-values.
lattice-gate~formalism-and-uncertainty.remember: Bloch's theorem: $H$ commutes with lattice translations, so eigenstates carry the translation eigenvalue $e^{ik a}$, and $k$ matters only modulo $2\pi/a$.

phonon-halls~radiative-transfer.story:
Heat flows from hot to cold because carriers move: some from the hot side carry more energy than those that arrive from the cold side. A simple kinetic estimate gives a thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\rm th}=\tfrac13 C\,v\,\ell$: $C$ is the heat capacity per volume (energy each carrier can carry), $v$ is the speed and $\ell$ the mean free path (the distance before a carrier scatters and forgets where it came from). The factor $\tfrac13$ comes from averaging over three directions.

In an insulating crystal (room A) the carriers are phonons, travelling at the speed of sound. In a star (room B) the carriers are photons: $v=c$ and $C_{\rm rad}=4aT^3$ from the Stefan-Boltzmann law, with $\ell=1/(\kappa\rho)$ set by the opacity. This gives $K_{\rm rad}=4acT^3/(3\kappa\rho)$ and a temperature gradient $dT/dr=-3\kappa\rho L/(16\pi acT^3r^2)$.

Same formula; what changes is who scatters what. For phonons it is Umklapp processes, defects and the boundaries of the sample; for photons it is absorption and electron scattering. At low temperature in a clean crystal $\ell$ is limited by the sample size and $\kappa_{\rm th}\propto T^3$, like $C$.
phonon-halls~radiative-transfer.example: In the radiative zone of a star the flux is fixed by the luminosity, $F=L/4\pi r^2$, and $F=-K_{\rm rad}\,dT/dr$. Double the opacity $\kappa$ and $K_{\rm rad}$ halves, so the temperature gradient must be twice as steep to carry the same $L$. A steeper gradient is what eventually triggers convection, which is why opaque layers become convective.
phonon-halls~radiative-transfer.remember: $\kappa_{\rm th}=\tfrac13 C\,v\,\ell$ for phonons and photons alike; for photons $C=4aT^3$, $v=c$, $\ell=1/(\kappa\rho)$.

degenerate-core~stellar-forge.story:
A normal star has a thermostat. If the core gets a little hotter, its pressure rises, the core expands, expansion cools it, and the fusion rate drops back. Stable. That works only because the pressure depends on temperature, $P=nk_BT$.

A degenerate gas lacks this feedback. Its pressure $P\approx\tfrac25nE_F$ depends on the density, not on $T$, as long as $T\ll T_F$. In the helium core of a red giant ($\rho_c\approx10^9$ kg/m$^3$) the electron density is $n=\rho/(\mu_em_u)=3.0\times10^{35}$ m$^{-3}$, with $E_F\approx0.16$ MeV and $T_F\approx1.9\times10^9$ K, far above the actual $T\approx10^8$ K.

Now ignite helium in the triple-alpha process, whose rate depends extremely steeply on temperature, $\varepsilon\propto T^{\sim40}$. The heat raises $T$, but the pressure hardly changes, so the core does not expand and does not cool. The higher $T$ raises the rate further, which heats more: a runaway, the helium flash. The thermostat only returns when the heating has lifted the core out of degeneracy ($T\sim T_F$).
degenerate-core~stellar-forge.example: At $T\approx10^8$ K the ratio is $T/T_F\approx0.05$, so the thermal correction to the pressure is $(T/T_F)^2\sim0.3\%$. Raise $T$ by $10\%$: the pressure is essentially unchanged, but the rate grows by $1.1^{40}\approx45$ times. An ideal gas at the same temperature would respond with a $10\%$ rise in pressure and would start expanding.
degenerate-core~stellar-forge.remember: Degenerate pressure does not depend on $T$, so a degenerate core cannot expand when heated: no negative feedback, hence the helium flash.

fermi-sea~early-universe.story:
Fermions and bosons with the same temperature fill their states differently. Bosons follow $1/(e^{x}-1)$ (Bose-Einstein), fermions $1/(e^{x}+1)$ (Fermi-Dirac), with $x=E/k_BT$. The $+1$ means the occupation can never exceed $1$ (Pauli), so fewer fermions fit in than bosons. For massless particles integrating gives $\int x^2/(e^x+1)=\tfrac34\int x^2/(e^x-1)$: a factor $\tfrac34$ in the number density and $\tfrac78$ in the energy density.

Room A is the metal, with the density of states $\propto\sqrt E$ and strong degeneracy. Room B is the early universe: neutrinos at temperatures of MeV are relativistic and have $\mu\approx0$, so they are thermal, not degenerate, but still obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. After the neutrinos decouple, electrons and positrons annihilate and heat only the photons, so $T_\nu=(4/11)^{1/3}T_\gamma=1.95$ K today. Together with the factor $\tfrac34$, that gives $n_\nu=\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac4{11}\,n_\gamma$ per species.

Same distribution function; the early-universe gas is in the opposite limit to a metal ($\mu\approx0$ instead of $\mu\gg k_BT$).
fermi-sea~early-universe.example: With $n_\gamma=411$ cm$^{-3}$ today, one species of neutrino plus its antineutrino has $n_\nu=\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac4{11}\cdot411=112$ cm$^{-3}$. For three species that is $336$ cm$^{-3}$, comparable to the photons. The relic neutrinos are about as numerous as the CMB photons but much colder: $1.95$ K against $2.725$ K, so they are far harder to detect.
fermi-sea~early-universe.remember: Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein differ by $\pm1$; for massless particles the integrals differ by $\tfrac34$ in number and $\tfrac78$ in energy; $T_\nu=(4/11)^{1/3}T_\gamma$.

magnet-vault~interstellar-medium.story:
In a magnetic field an atomic level with total angular momentum $F$ splits into sublevels labelled by $m_F$, whose energies change by $g_Fm_F\mu_BB$. A spectral line between such levels therefore splits into components at slightly different frequencies. This Zeeman splitting measures $B$. The same atomic physics works on Earth (room A) and in space (room B): the atom does not know where it is.

Room B uses the 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen. The upper level $F=1$ splits into $m_F=0,\pm1$, with a shift of $1.4$ Hz per microgauss ($\mu$G) for each component. The two circularly polarised components, $\sigma_+$ and $\sigma_-$, are shifted in opposite directions, so the splitting between them is $2.8$ Hz/$\mu$G.

The catch is that typical fields in the interstellar medium are only a few $\mu$G, while the line is broadened by thermal motion to about $1$ km/s $\approx5$ kHz. The splitting is thousands of times smaller than the line width, so one cannot see two lines. Instead, astronomers measure the difference between right- and left-circularly polarised light (Stokes $V$), which is proportional to $B_\parallel\,dI/d\nu$: the slope of the line profile, times the field along the line of sight.
magnet-vault~interstellar-medium.example: A field of $B=5\ \mu$G shifts each component by $\approx7$ Hz. The thermal Doppler width of $1$ km/s corresponds to $\Delta\nu=(v/c)\,\nu_0=4.7$ kHz, so the shift is $1.5\times10^{-3}$ of the width. It is invisible as a split but detectable as a small difference between the two polarisations measured with long integration times.
magnet-vault~interstellar-medium.remember: Zeeman splitting $\Delta\nu=g_F\mu_BB/h=1.4$ MHz/G measures interstellar fields, but the shift is tiny compared with the width, so one measures circular polarisation $V\propto B_\parallel\,dI/d\nu$.

semiconductor-forge~photometry-radiation.story:
A semiconductor has a forbidden energy gap $E_g$ between its filled valence band and its empty conduction band. A photon can lift an electron across the gap, creating a mobile electron-hole pair, only if its energy is at least the gap: $h\nu\ge E_g$. Photons with less energy pass straight through. In wavelength terms, absorption stops for $\lambda>\lambda_g=hc/E_g=1.2398\ \mu\text{m}/(E_g/\text{eV})$.

Room A is the physics of the gap. Room B is the astronomer's detector: a CCD is a piece of silicon, and each absorbed photon frees an electron that is counted. Its quantum efficiency (the fraction of photons detected) falls to zero beyond $\lambda_g$. That is why silicon CCDs cannot see much beyond $1\ \mu$m, and why infrared astronomy uses narrow-gap materials such as Ge or HgCdTe. The filter bands (U, B, V, R, I) tell which part of the spectrum you collect, and magnitudes $m=-2.5\log_{10}F+\text{const}$ are then compared across bands.

The same relation, read backwards, tells you the colour of a light-emitting diode: the photon energy emitted is about the gap.
semiconductor-forge~photometry-radiation.example: Silicon: $E_g=1.12$ eV, so $\lambda_g=1.2398/1.12=1.107\ \mu$m. A photon at $1.3\ \mu$m carries only $0.95$ eV, below the gap, and is not detected. GaAs ($1.42$ eV) has $\lambda_g=0.873\ \mu$m. For an LED the logic is reversed: a gap of $1.9$ eV gives red light at $\lambda\approx650$ nm, a gap of $3.1$ eV gives violet-blue at about $400$ nm.
semiconductor-forge~photometry-radiation.remember: The photon is absorbed only if $h\nu\ge E_g$, i.e. $\lambda\le\lambda_g=1.2398\ \mu\text{m}/(E_g/\text{eV})$: this sets the CCD red cut-off and the LED colour.

drift-corridor~interstellar-medium.story:
Free charges respond to an oscillating electric field by sloshing back and forth. The electron cloud of a metal does it collectively, at the plasma frequency $\omega_p=\sqrt{ne^2/\epsilon_0m}$: it is the natural frequency at which a cloud of electrons displaced against a fixed positive background oscillates. Where the density $n$ is larger, the restoring force is stronger and $\omega_p$ is higher.

If a wave has $\omega<\omega_p$, the electrons can follow it and cancel the field: the dielectric function $\epsilon(\omega)=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$ is negative, and the wave cannot propagate, it is reflected. That is why metals are shiny and why the ionosphere reflects short-wave radio. If $\omega>\omega_p$ the electrons cannot follow, the wave goes through, but with a group velocity $v_g=c\sqrt{1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2}$ slightly below $c$.

Room A is the electron gas of a metal; room B is the dilute ionised gas between the stars. Only the density differs by some $24$ orders of magnitude. A pulsar emits a sharp pulse over a wide band of frequencies; the lower frequencies travel slower through the plasma and arrive later. The delay is $\Delta t\propto\mathrm{DM}/\nu^2$, where the dispersion measure $\mathrm{DM}=\int n_e\,dl$ is the electron column density.
drift-corridor~interstellar-medium.example: For pulsar signals with $\mathrm{DM}=50$ pc cm$^{-3}$ the delay is $\Delta t=4.15\text{ ms}\times50/\nu^2$ ($\nu$ in GHz): $106$ ms at $1.4$ GHz and $424$ ms at $0.7$ GHz. Halving the frequency quadruples the delay. The plasma frequency of the interstellar gas with $n_e=0.03$ cm$^{-3}$ is only $1.6$ kHz, far below radio frequencies, so waves pass through easily. In copper $\hbar\omega_p\approx10.8$ eV, in the ultraviolet.
drift-corridor~interstellar-medium.remember: Plasma frequency $\omega_p^2=ne^2/\epsilon_0m$: waves below it are reflected, above it propagate at $v_g<c$, causing the frequency-dependent pulsar delay $\propto\mathrm{DM}/\nu^2$.

harmonic-oscillator-elevator~photometry-.story:
A mode of the electromagnetic field in a box is mathematically a harmonic oscillator. Its quantum states are labelled by $n$: the number of photons in that mode, each with energy $\hbar\omega$. The raising operator $a^\dagger$ adds a photon, $a$ removes one, and $a^\dagger a$ counts them.

At temperature $T$ the mode is in thermal equilibrium, and the probability for $n$ photons is proportional to $e^{-n\hbar\omega/k_BT}$. Summing that gives the average number $ ar n=1/(e^{h
u/k_BT}-1)$ (room A). Room B multiplies by the energy per photon and the number of modes to get the blackbody intensity $B_
u=(2h
u^3/c^2)\, ar n_
u$.

Two limits. If $h
u\ll k_BT$ the mode holds many photons, $ ar n\approx k_BT/h
u\gg1$, and the field behaves like a classical wave (Rayleigh-Jeans). If $h
u\gg k_BT$ the mode is almost always empty, $ ar n\approx e^{-h
u/k_BT}\ll1$: it is a rare event to find even one photon (Wien tail).

So the same $ ar n$ is a classical field amplitude in the radio and a rare quantum in the ultraviolet.
harmonic-oscillator-elevator~photometry-.example: In the CMB ($T=2.725$ K), a radio mode at $1.4$ GHz has $h\nu/k_BT=0.025$, so $\bar n\approx40$ photons: classical. In sunlight ($5800$ K) a green mode at $500$ nm has $h\nu/k_BT=4.96$ and $\bar n\approx0.007$: on average, one photon in about $140$ modes. Same formula, completely different character.
harmonic-oscillator-elevator~photometry-.remember: The thermal occupation $\bar n=1/(e^{h\nu/k_BT}-1)$ of a radiation mode is the mean quantum number of an oscillator: many photons classical, almost none in the Wien tail.

tunneling-bridge~semiconductor-forge.story:
In a reverse-biased, heavily doped p-n junction the electric field tilts the energy bands. Between the valence band (full of electrons) and the conduction band (empty) lies the gap, which classically is a forbidden zone. But if the field $\mathcal E$ is strong, the conduction band edge at some place lies at the same energy as the valence band edge a short distance away, and an electron can tunnel through the gap: the Zener effect.

Room A is the tunnelling calculation for a barrier that is not rectangular. Here the potential energy of the electron in the gap falls linearly with position, so the barrier is triangular, with height $E_g-e\mathcal Ex$. The width is $L=E_g/e\mathcal E$: the stronger the field, the narrower the barrier. The WKB integral $2\int\kappa\,dx$ over this triangle gives the exponent $\frac{4\sqrt{2m^*}E_g^{3/2}}{3e\hbar\mathcal E}$. So the current is $I\propto e^{-b/\mathcal E}$, with the constant $b$ built from the effective mass $m^*$ and the gap.

Compared with a plain rectangular barrier, a stronger field helps twice: it narrows the barrier and makes it shallower. The result is a very sharp threshold in the field, used in Zener diodes as voltage references.
tunneling-bridge~semiconductor-forge.example: The exponent is $-b/\mathcal E$, where $b=4\sqrt{2m^*}E_g^{3/2}/(3e\hbar)$. For silicon ($E_g=1.12$ eV, $m^*=0.2m_e$) $b\approx3.6\times10^9$ V/m. At a field $\mathcal E=2\times10^8$ V/m the exponent is about $-18$. Doubling the field to $4\times10^8$ V/m changes it to $-9$ and the current rises by $e^{9}\approx8000$. A small voltage step turns the junction from off to on.
tunneling-bridge~semiconductor-forge.remember: Zener tunnelling = WKB through a triangular barrier of height $E_g$ and width $E_g/e\mathcal E$, giving $I\propto e^{-b/\mathcal E}$.

angular-momentum-spin~degenerate-matter.story:
Every neutron and every electron has spin $1/2$, which means its spin has exactly $2s+1=2$ possible states, "up" and "down". The Pauli principle says that no two identical fermions can share the same complete quantum state. In a box, a complete state is a wave vector $\mathbf k$ together with a spin direction. So every point in $k$-space can hold two particles, not one: $g_s=2$.

Room A (QM) provides this counting rule. Room B uses it for the neutron star. The number density is the number of states in the Fermi ball per volume: $n=g_s\frac{4\pi k_F^3/3}{(2\pi)^3}=\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2}$, so $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$. With nuclear density $n_0=0.16$ fm$^{-3}$ this gives $k_F=1.68$ fm$^{-1}$ and $E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m_n\approx58$ MeV.

If the counting factor were wrong, all results would shift. Had the particles integer spin (bosons), they could all pile into the lowest state and there would be no degeneracy pressure at all.
angular-momentum-spin~degenerate-matter.example: Suppose neutrons had only one spin state per $\mathbf k$ ($g_s=1$) at the same density. Then $k_F$ would be larger by $2^{1/3}=1.26$ and $E_F$ by $2^{2/3}=1.59$: $E_F\approx93$ MeV instead of $58$ MeV. In symmetric nuclear matter with protons and neutrons together ($g=4$) at the same total density $k_F=1.33$ fm$^{-1}$.
angular-momentum-spin~degenerate-matter.remember: Spin $1/2$ gives two states per $\mathbf k$-point, so $n=k_F^3/3\pi^2$; every Fermi-gas result (metal, white dwarf, neutron star) uses this factor of 2.

perturbation-forge~radiative-transfer.story:
An excited atom in empty space emits a photon after a while, seemingly on its own. Quantum mechanics explains it: the atom couples to the electromagnetic field, which has modes available even when no photon is present. This coupling is a small perturbation. Time-dependent perturbation theory gives the rate to jump into a continuum of final states (Fermi's golden rule): rate $\propto|\text{matrix element}|^2\times$ the density of final states.

For a photon the matrix element is the dipole moment $\mathbf d_{12}=-e\langle1|\mathbf r|2\rangle$ and the density of photon states grows as $\omega^2$. Together with one more factor $\omega$ from the field strength this gives $A_{21}=\omega^3|\mathbf d_{12}|^2/(3\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c^3)$: room A. Room B takes it up in radiative transfer. Einstein had introduced $A_{21}$ (spontaneous emission) and $B_{21}$, $B_{12}$ (stimulated emission, absorption) from thermodynamics, and they are related: $g_1B_{12}=g_2B_{21}$ and $B_{21}=c^3A_{21}/(8\pi h\nu^3)$. Quantum mechanics calculates one of them, then all follow.

That is why astronomers can use the emissivity $j_\nu=\frac{h\nu}{4\pi}n_2A_{21}\phi(\nu)$ with a number from atomic physics.
perturbation-forge~radiative-transfer.example: For Lyman alpha the matrix element is $\langle1s|z|2p_0\rangle=\frac{128\sqrt2}{243}a_0=0.745\,a_0$ and $\omega=0.75\,\mathrm{Ry}/\hbar=1.55\times10^{16}$ s$^{-1}$. The formula gives $A_{21}=6.27\times10^8$ s$^{-1}$, i.e. a lifetime of $1.6$ ns. Because $A\propto\omega^3$, a transition with the same dipole moment but half the frequency would live $8$ times longer.
perturbation-forge~radiative-transfer.remember: Fermi's golden rule (matrix element squared times density of photon states $\propto\omega^2$) gives $A_{21}\propto\omega^3|d|^2$, and the Einstein relations give $B_{21}$.

formalism-and-uncertainty~radiative-tran.story:
An excited state does not live forever: it decays with a lifetime $	au=1/A$. The energy-time uncertainty relation says that a state that exists only for time $	au$ has an energy uncertain by $\Delta E\sim\hbar/	au$. So the emitted photons are not exactly at $
u_0$ but have a spread, a Lorentzian profile of full width $\Delta
u_{m nat}=A/2\pi$. Its shape decreases only as $1/(
u-
u_0)^2$ in the wings. This is the natural line width (room A).

Room B: in a hot gas the atoms move with Maxwell-distributed velocities, and the Doppler effect shifts the frequency of the light each atom absorbs. Many atoms with different velocities produce a Gaussian profile of width $\Delta
u_D=
u_0\sqrt{2k_BT/m_Hc^2}$, which falls off exponentially.

Both effects act together, so the profile is the convolution of the two, the Voigt profile. The Gaussian dominates the centre (the core) of the line, because it is much wider. Far from the centre the Gaussian dies exponentially while the Lorentzian only falls as a power law, so the wings come from natural broadening. That is why absorption lines have broad wings.
formalism-and-uncertainty~radiative-tran.example: For Lyman alpha $A=6.27\times10^8$ s$^{-1}$, so $\Delta\nu_{\rm nat}=A/2\pi=100$ MHz (equivalent to $\Delta E=\hbar/\tau=4\times10^{-7}$ eV with $\tau=1.6$ ns). At $T=10^4$ K the Doppler width is $\Delta\nu_D=106$ GHz: the Doppler core is $1000$ times wider, so natural broadening shows only in the far wings.
formalism-and-uncertainty~radiative-tran.remember: Natural width $A/2\pi$ (from $\Delta E\,\tau\sim\hbar$) gives Lorentzian wings; thermal Doppler motion gives a Gaussian core; together they form the Voigt profile.

wave-mechanics-basics~degenerate-core.story:
When do quantum effects matter for a gas of particles? A particle with momentum $p$ is a wave of wavelength $h/p$. For a thermal gas the typical wavelength is the thermal de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{\rm th}=h/\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}$: the hotter, the shorter. If the particles are far apart compared with $\lambda_{\rm th}$, they behave like separate billiard balls and classical statistics works. If $\lambda_{\rm th}$ becomes comparable to the typical spacing $n^{-1/3}$, the waves overlap, particles of the same kind are no longer distinguishable, and quantum statistics (Fermi-Dirac or Bose-Einstein) must be used.

So the criterion is the dimensionless number $n\lambda_{\rm th}^3$. If it is $\gg1$ the gas is degenerate, which is equivalent to $T\ll T_F\sim\hbar^2n^{2/3}/mk_B$. If it is $\ll1$ the gas is classical. A light particle (small $m$), a high density or a low temperature all push towards degeneracy.

Both solid-state electrons (room B, left) and the electrons in a stellar core (room B, right) are tested with this criterion.
wave-mechanics-basics~degenerate-core.example: Copper electrons at $300$ K: $\lambda_{\rm th}=4.3$ nm, much larger than the spacing $n^{-1/3}=0.23$ nm, so $n\lambda_{\rm th}^3=6.7\times10^3$: strongly degenerate. Nitrogen gas at $300$ K: $\lambda_{\rm th}=0.019$ nm, $n\lambda_{\rm th}^3=1.7\times10^{-7}$: classical. Heating the copper electrons to about $10^5$ K would be needed to shrink $\lambda_{\rm th}$ to the spacing, near $T_F=8.2\times10^4$ K.
wave-mechanics-basics~degenerate-core.remember: Quantum statistics matter when $n\lambda_{\rm th}^3\gtrsim1$, i.e. when matter waves overlap: below $T_F$, for light particles at high density.

phonon-halls~fermi-sea.story:
A metal stores heat in two ways: in lattice vibrations (phonons) and in its conduction electrons. At low temperature both contributions are known. Phonons: $C_{ph}=\beta T^3$ (Debye, from room A), with $\beta=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}R/\Theta_D^3$. Electrons: $C_{el}=\gamma T$ (Sommerfeld, from room B), with $\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{2}R/T_F$ for free electrons. The total is $C=\gamma T+\beta T^3$.

Why the different powers? Phonons are bosons whose number grows as $T^3$ (more modes become active as $T$ rises). Electrons are fermions of which only a fraction $T/T_F$ can take up heat, which gives a linear law. At very low temperature the linear term wins; at higher temperature the cubic one.

In practice one plots $C/T$ against $T^2$: $C/T=\gamma+\beta T^2$ is a straight line. The intercept gives $\gamma$ (and so the density of states at $E_F$, and an effective mass), and the slope gives $\beta$ (and so the Debye temperature). One graph delivers both numbers, which is why it appears in exam problems.
phonon-halls~fermi-sea.example: Copper: $\Theta_D=343$ K gives $\beta=4.8\times10^{-5}$ J/(mol K$^4$). The measured $\gamma=0.695$ mJ/(mol K$^2$) is higher than the free-electron value $0.50$ mJ/(mol K$^2$), so $m^*/m=1.4$. At $T=1$ K, $C_{el}=0.695$ mJ and $C_{ph}=0.048$ mJ, electrons dominate. They are equal at $T_c=\sqrt{\gamma/\beta}\approx3.8$ K.
phonon-halls~fermi-sea.remember: $C=\gamma T+\beta T^3$: electrons (fermions, fraction $T/T_F$) give the linear term, phonons (bosons) the cubic one; plot $C/T$ against $T^2$.

nuclear-furnace~stellar-forge.story:
Fusion rate depends on two things pulling in opposite directions. The number of particles with a given energy $E$ falls as $e^{-E/k_BT}$ (few particles are fast). The tunnelling probability through the Coulomb barrier rises with energy as $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$. The product has a narrow maximum at an energy $E_0$ well above $k_BT$ but well below the barrier: the Gamow peak. Almost all fusions happen there.

Evaluating the integral around the peak (the saddle point method) gives a rate that is approximately a power law in temperature, $\langle\sigma vangle\propto T^
u$, with $
u=(	au-2)/3$ and $	au=3(E_G/4k_BT)^{1/3}$. Larger $E_G$ (more charge on the nuclei) means a larger exponent $
u$: the more charged the nuclei, the more sensitive the rate is to $T$.

Room B uses this in stellar structure, where the energy generation is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0ho T^
u$. For the pp chain $
u\approx4$. For the CNO cycle ($^{14}$N plus a proton, $Z_1Z_2=7$) $
u\approx20$. A high exponent means the energy production is concentrated in the very centre. That requires a steep temperature gradient to carry the heat, which favours convection in the cores of heavier stars.
nuclear-furnace~stellar-forge.example:
Raise the core temperature of a star by $10\%$. For the pp chain with $
u\approx4$ the rate grows by $1.1^4\approx1.46$. For the CNO cycle with $
u\approx20$ it grows by $1.1^{20}\approx6.7$. The numbers: pp has $E_G=493$ keV, $	au=13.7$ and $
u=3.9$ at $1.5	imes10^7$ K; CNO has $E_G=44.8$ MeV, $	au=61.6$ and $
u=19.9$.
nuclear-furnace~stellar-forge.remember: The Gamow peak (Boltzmann tail times tunnelling) gives $\langle\sigma v\rangle\propto T^\nu$ with $\nu=(\tau-2)/3$; a higher barrier gives a steeper $T$-dependence.
